text: We design single-shot shaped pulses for ultra-high-fidelity population transfer in a three-level quantum system with a lambda configuration. This construction provides analytical control over the evolution rather than relying solely on numerical pulse optimization. Within this family, we identify a one-parameter tracking solution that jointly controls transfer fidelity, excited-state occupation, and robustness. The single parameter therefore exposes the trade-offs among three experimentally important performance measures. Robustness is quantified by the minimum percentage change in pulse area required to increase infidelity beyond $10^{-4}$. text: Online reviews provide product evaluations that influence consumer purchasing decisions and can therefore affect both individual purchases and broader market outcomes. These evaluations can be manipulated, however, by professional spammers who publish fraudulent reviews and continually adapt their tactics to deployed detection systems. The adversarial nature of this process means that a detector trained against one known strategy may become ineffective when spammers change their behavior. Modeling such activity is difficult because strategies evolve rapidly, differ across spammers and target products, and are generally unknown in advance. In addition, most existing detectors optimize classification accuracy, an objective that does not directly capture the broader goal of preserving trustworthy product evaluations. A highly accurate classifier may still fail to protect the aggregate scores and rankings that consumers ultimately observe. To address these limitations, we formulate a minimax game in which spammers and detectors compete under practical objectives extending beyond accuracy alone. The resulting Nash equilibria produce stable detectors that remain effective against arbitrary mixtures of spamming strategies, providing robustness even when the attacker’s exact behavior is not known beforehand.

text: I want to discuss the future of money by beginning with the Yapese, a Micronesian culture in the early twentieth century. Their form of currency is especially fascinating because it demonstrates that money does not need to be portable, physically exchanged, or even immediately accessible in order to function. They do not carry or exchange these stones as we do coins because some are enormous; the largest weighs roughly four tons and measures twelve feet across. Moving such an object for every transaction would be impossible. Instead, the community collectively records who owns each stone or share of a stone. Ownership changes through shared knowledge and agreement, even while the physical stone remains where it is. One story tells of sailors transporting a Rai stone across the ocean when they encountered trouble and the stone fell overboard. Although it was no longer visible or recoverable, the community continued to recognize its existence and ownership because everyone accepted the account of what had happened.
